title: Acts Chapter 25 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Acts chapter 25 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Acts Chapter 25 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Acts Chapter 25.

questions.question: In Acts 25, which of the following appears FIRST in the chapter?
options: Festus ascended from Caesarea to Jerusalem
The high priest informed Festus against Paul
Festus commanded Paul to be brought
questions.correctAnswer: Festus ascended from Caesarea to Jerusalem
questions.explanation: This event is stated in Acts 25:1, which describes Festus coming into the province and ascending to Jerusalem.

questions.question: Who informed Festus against Paul?
questions.explanation: Acts 25:2 states that the high priest and the chief of the Jews informed Festus against Paul.

questions.question: What did the high priest and the chief of the Jews desire from Festus?
questions.explanation: Acts 25:3 indicates that they besought Festus to send for Paul to Jerusalem.

questions.question: What did Festus decide regarding Paul?
options: Paul should be sent to Jerusalem
Paul should be kept at Caesarea
questions.correctAnswer: Paul should be kept at Caesarea
questions.explanation: In Acts 25:4, Festus clearly states that Paul should be kept at Caesarea.

questions.question: What did Festus ask those able among the Jews to do?
questions.explanation: Acts 25:5 shows that Festus asked those able among the Jews to go down with him to accuse Paul.

questions.question: How long did Festus tarry among the Jews?
questions.explanation: Acts 25:6 states that Festus tarried among them more than ten days before going down to Caesarea.

questions.question: What did the Jews do when Festus commanded Paul to be brought?
questions.explanation: Acts 25:7 indicates that the Jews stood round about when Paul was brought before Festus.

questions.question: What did Paul say he had not offended against?
questions.explanation: In Acts 25:8, Paul states that he has not offended against the law of the Jews, the temple, or Caesar.

questions.question: What did Festus wish to do concerning the Jews?
questions.explanation: Acts 25:9 reveals that Festus, willing to do the Jews a pleasure, asked Paul if he would go up to Jerusalem.

questions.question: Was Paul accused of grievous complaints?
questions.explanation: Acts 25:7 states that the Jews laid many and grievous complaints against Paul.

questions.question: Did Paul have any offense against the temple?
options: He was not accused of this
questions.explanation: According to Acts 25:8, Paul asserted that he had not offended against the temple at all.

questions.question: Festus asked Paul if he would go up to Jerusalem, didn't he?
questions.explanation: This is confirmed in Acts 25:9 where Festus asks Paul if he would go up to Jerusalem.

questions.question: The chief of the Jews desired to have Paul killed.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:3 indicates that they desired favor against Paul, laying wait to kill him.

questions.question: Festus kept Paul in Jerusalem.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:4 states that Festus kept Paul at Caesarea, not in Jerusalem.

questions.question: Paul was proven guilty of grievous complaints.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:7 mentions that the complaints against Paul could not be proven.

medium.title: Acts Chapter 25 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Acts Chapter 25 to real-life situations.

questions.question: What did Paul declare he was doing at Caesar's judgment seat?
questions.explanation: Paul stated, 'I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged' (Acts 25:10) to assert his right to a fair hearing.

questions.question: What does Acts 25:11 promise will happen if someone refuses to die for an offense they did not commit?
options: They will be delivered to the Jews
questions.explanation: In Acts 25:11, Paul indicates that if he has not committed any offense worthy of death, he will appeal unto Caesar.

questions.question: What was Festus' response to Paul's appeal to Caesar?
questions.explanation: Festus conferred with the council before answering, 'Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go' (Acts 25:12).

questions.question: What was the purpose of King Agrippa's visit to Caesarea?
options: To confer with the Jewish leaders
questions.explanation: Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea to salute Festus as stated in Acts 25:13.

questions.question: What did Festus declare to King Agrippa about Paul?
options: He has committed a serious crime
There is a certain man left in bonds by Felix
questions.correctAnswer: There is a certain man left in bonds by Felix
questions.explanation: Festus informed King Agrippa that there is a certain man left in bonds by Felix, indicating Paul's situation (Acts 25:14).

questions.question: What did the chief priests and elders desire concerning Paul?
questions.explanation: The chief priests and elders sought judgment against Paul, as Festus explained (Acts 25:15).

questions.question: What principle did Festus state regarding Roman law?
options: No man should be judged without a trial
The accused must face their accusers
questions.explanation: Festus explained that it is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die without facing the accusers and being able to defend himself (Acts 25:16).

questions.question: What did Festus do the day after the accusers came?
options: He sat on the judgment seat
questions.correctAnswer: He sat on the judgment seat
questions.explanation: Festus sat on the judgment seat the day after the accusers came, demonstrating his role in the proceedings (Acts 25:17).

questions.question: What did the accusers fail to do when standing up against Paul?
options: They brought none accusation of such things as I supposed
questions.correctAnswer: They brought none accusation of such things as I supposed
questions.explanation: Festus noted that against Paul, the accusers brought none of the accusations he expected (Acts 25:18).

questions.question: How should Christians respond to wrongful accusations, as exemplified by Paul?
questions.explanation: Paul's appeal to Caesar reflects a trust in God's justice and the legal process, encouraging Christians to remain faithful in the face of wrongful accusations.

questions.question: What principle can we learn about facing trials from Festus' statement on accusations?
questions.explanation: Festus’ statement highlights the principle that justice requires evidence, and that accusations must be taken seriously while acknowledging the reality of wrongful accusations.

questions.question: What can we learn about authority from Festus' interactions with Paul?
questions.explanation: Despite injustices, Festus’ role as a Roman leader shows that authority must be respected, reflecting the Christian principle of submitting to governing authorities (Romans 13:1).

questions.question: Is it important to face one's accusers according to biblical principles?
questions.explanation: Acts 25:16 indicates that facing accusers is a principle of justice that is upheld in both Roman law and biblical ethics.

questions.question: Should Christians avoid appealing to legal authorities when wronged?
questions.explanation: Paul’s appeal to Caesar shows that it is acceptable for Christians to seek justice through legal authorities when facing wrongful accusations.

questions.question: Is it acceptable for Christians to be silent in the face of wrongful accusations?
questions.explanation: While silence can be a strategy, Acts 25 shows the importance of defending oneself and seeking justice, as Paul did.

hard.title: Acts Chapter 25 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Acts Chapter 25.

questions.question: What did Paul affirm about Jesus in Acts 25:19?
questions.explanation: This is correct as Paul affirmed that Jesus, who was dead, was indeed alive (Acts 25:19).

questions.question: What did Festus doubt regarding Paul's case in Acts 25:20?
questions.explanation: Festus doubted the nature of the questions concerning Paul, indicating uncertainty about the Jewish accusations (Acts 25:20).

questions.question: Why did Festus command Paul to be kept until he could send him to Caesar, as stated in Acts 25:21?
options: To protect Paul from the Jews
questions.explanation: Festus kept Paul because he had appealed to be reserved for the hearing of Augustus (Acts 25:21).

questions.question: What was King Agrippa's response regarding Paul in Acts 25:22?
options: He wanted to judge Paul immediately
He wanted to hear Paul himself
He refused to listen to Paul
questions.correctAnswer: He wanted to hear Paul himself
questions.explanation: Agrippa expressed his desire to hear Paul personally, indicating his interest in the case (Acts 25:22).

questions.question: In Acts 25:24, what did Festus say about the multitude of the Jews?
questions.explanation: Festus indicated that the multitude of the Jews had been demanding Paul's death (Acts 25:24).

questions.question: What did Festus find regarding Paul's actions in Acts 25:25?
questions.explanation: Festus determined that Paul had committed nothing worthy of death, which is why he decided to send him (Acts 25:25).

questions.question: What does the Greek word 'superstition' in Acts 25:19 mean?
questions.explanation: The term refers to irrational or excessive belief in the supernatural, aligning closely with idolatry (Acts 25:19).

questions.question: Which literary device is used in Acts 25:24 where Festus addresses Agrippa and the assembly?
questions.explanation: Festus directly addresses Agrippa and the assembly, a common technique in oratory to engage the audience (Acts 25:24).

questions.question: Which other Bible passage connects to the theme of unjust accusations as seen in Acts 25:19?
questions.explanation: Psalm 35:11 speaks of false witnesses rising against the innocent, paralleling the unjust accusations faced by Paul (Acts 25:19).

questions.question: Which passage fulfills the theme of legal appeals found in Acts 25:21?
questions.explanation: In Acts 22:25, Paul appeals to his rights as a Roman citizen, similar to his appeal in Acts 25:21.

questions.question: What precedes the events of Acts 25:19?
questions.explanation: The context leading to Acts 25:19 is the grievous accusations laid out against Paul by the Jews (Acts 25:18).

questions.question: What follows Acts 25:23 where Agrippa arrives with Bernice?
questions.explanation: Festus begins to present Paul's case to Agrippa after his arrival (Acts 25:24).

questions.question: The mention of 'Augustus' in Acts 25:21 refers to what type of authority?
questions.explanation: Augustus refers to the title of the first Roman emperor, indicating the highest authority in the Roman legal system (Acts 25:21).

questions.question: Is it true that Festus found Paul guilty of any crime in Acts 25:25?
questions.explanation: Festus found that Paul had committed nothing worthy of death, thus he was not guilty (Acts 25:25).

questions.question: Is it false that Agrippa expressed interest in hearing Paul in Acts 25:22?
questions.explanation: Agrippa indeed expressed a desire to hear Paul, which makes the statement false (Acts 25:22).

theological.title: Acts Chapter 25 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Acts Chapter 25 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What doctrine does Acts 25:8 teach about human sin and innocence before divine and human law?
options: Paul claims he has not offended against the law of the Jews, the temple, nor Caesar, illustrating the possibility of innocence in human judgment.
Paul admits guilt before the Jewish law but innocence before Roman law, showing partial human sinfulness.
Paul denies all charges but confesses to sins unknown to the authorities, emphasizing hidden sinfulness.
Paul appeals to divine mercy rather than asserting innocence, highlighting human sinfulness in all courts.
questions.correctAnswer: Paul claims he has not offended against the law of the Jews, the temple, nor Caesar, illustrating the possibility of innocence in human judgment.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:8 records Paul’s defense that he has not offended any law, demonstrating a doctrinal principle that innocence before human legal systems is possible and significant in divine providence.

questions.question: What doctrine does Acts 25:11 teach about the believer's right to divine justice and appeal?
options: Paul’s appeal to Caesar illustrates the believer’s right to seek justice under sovereign authority when accused unjustly.
Paul’s refusal to appeal represents submission to earthly powers without resistance.
Paul’s acceptance of death without appeal shows the doctrine of redemptive suffering.
Paul’s appeal to Jewish leaders demonstrates the primacy of religious courts over civil authorities.
questions.correctAnswer: Paul’s appeal to Caesar illustrates the believer’s right to seek justice under sovereign authority when accused unjustly.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:11 shows Paul appealing to Caesar to avoid unjust local judgment, teaching the doctrine that believers may rightly seek justice under higher authorities ordained by God.

questions.question: What doctrine does Acts 25:16 teach about Roman legal procedure and the right to a fair trial?
options: It teaches the doctrine of the right to confront accusers and defend oneself before judgment.
It teaches the doctrine of absolute power of Roman governors to execute without trial.
It teaches that Jewish law supersedes Roman law in capital cases.
It teaches that Roman trials are based solely on written accusations without face-to-face confrontation.
questions.correctAnswer: It teaches the doctrine of the right to confront accusers and defend oneself before judgment.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:16 explains Roman legal customs requiring accusers to appear face to face with the accused, affirming the doctrine of due process and fair trial rights.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Acts 25:4 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: In Acts 25:4, Festus’s decision to keep Paul at Caesarea and control the legal process demonstrates God’s sovereignty working through human authorities.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Acts 25:12 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Acts 25:12 shows Festus consulting the council and affirming Paul’s right to appeal to Caesar, reflecting the attribute of justice in legal fairness.

questions.question: How does Acts 25:13–14 connect to the broader narrative arc of divine providence in Paul's mission?
options: It shows God orchestrating political events to bring Paul before rulers, fulfilling the spread of the Gospel.
It demonstrates human failure to recognize divine authority, ending Paul’s mission.
It reveals Paul’s rejection by all authorities, indicating the Gospel’s limitation.
It illustrates the futility of human governance without divine intervention.
questions.correctAnswer: It shows God orchestrating political events to bring Paul before rulers, fulfilling the spread of the Gospel.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:13–14 places Paul before King Agrippa and Bernice, demonstrating God's providential orchestration to advance the Gospel through political means.

questions.question: How does the interaction in Acts 25:23–24 prepare for the fulfillment of redemption history in the trial of Jesus and Paul?
options: It parallels Jesus’ unjust trials, highlighting continued rejection of Messiah and His witnesses.
It shows the triumph of human justice over divine injustice.
It contrasts Paul’s innocence with Jesus’ guilt, fulfilling condemnation.
It reveals the ultimate failure of the Jewish leaders to prosecute true criminals.
questions.correctAnswer: It parallels Jesus’ unjust trials, highlighting continued rejection of Messiah and His witnesses.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:23–24 shows Paul facing accusations and rejection similar to Jesus’ trials, preparing for the narrative of Messiah’s suffering and witness.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do verses Acts 25:11 and Acts 25:12 teach about Christian submission to civil authority and divine justice?
options: Believers have a God-given right to appeal to higher authorities when local judgment is unjust.
Believers must always accept local judgment without appeal.
Believers should avoid secular courts to maintain spiritual purity.
Believers are exempt from civil authority when accused falsely.
questions.correctAnswer: Believers have a God-given right to appeal to higher authorities when local judgment is unjust.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:11 shows Paul’s personal appeal to Caesar, and 25:12 confirms Festus’s acceptance of this appeal, teaching the doctrine of lawful Christian submission and appeal within civil systems.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do verses Acts 25:16 and Acts 25:18 teach about the integrity and limitations of human legal systems in judgment?
options: Human legal systems require procedural fairness but can be limited by ignorance or superstition.
Human legal systems are infallible and always reveal divine truth.
Human legal systems reject all religious questions as irrelevant.
Human legal systems provide immediate and absolute justice without error.
questions.correctAnswer: Human legal systems require procedural fairness but can be limited by ignorance or superstition.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:16 states the Roman right to confront accusers, while 25:18 shows accusations were based on superstition, illustrating fairness alongside human limitations.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do verses Acts 25:19 and Acts 25:21 teach about the resurrection and the witness of Christ through Paul’s trials?
options: Paul’s affirmation of the living Jesus amidst accusations of superstition underscores the doctrine of the resurrection as central to Christian witness.
Paul denies the resurrection to avoid trouble, showing compromise in witness.
Paul’s silence on resurrection shows its irrelevance to legal trials.
Paul accepts superstition as a neutral topic unrelated to salvation.
questions.correctAnswer: Paul’s affirmation of the living Jesus amidst accusations of superstition underscores the doctrine of the resurrection as central to Christian witness.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:19 records accusations involving Jesus who Paul says is alive, and 25:21 shows Paul’s appeal related to these matters, emphasizing resurrection doctrine.

questions.question: Sceptics claim that Acts 25:7–9 reveals that Festus was biased and unjust in his judgment of Paul. What does Acts 25:7–12 actually teach about Festus’ role and impartiality?
options: Festus tries to please the Jews but ultimately respects Paul’s right to a fair trial and allows his appeal to Caesar.
Festus immediately condemns Paul without hearing his defense.
Festus ignores Roman legal procedure and arbitrarily sends Paul to Jerusalem.
Festus refuses to act and leaves Paul’s case unresolved indefinitely.
questions.correctAnswer: Festus tries to please the Jews but ultimately respects Paul’s right to a fair trial and allows his appeal to Caesar.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:7–9 shows Festus offering to send Paul to Jerusalem to please the Jews, but verses 11–12 show he honors Paul’s appeal to Caesar, affirming legal fairness.

questions.question: What doctrine does Acts 25:1 teach about God’s providential timing in redemptive history?
options: God’s providence governs the timing of rulers arriving and events unfolding according to divine plan.
God is indifferent to political changes and leaves history to chance.
God’s plan is hindered by human political delays and uncertainties.
Human political events oppose God’s purposes without any divine control.
questions.correctAnswer: God’s providence governs the timing of rulers arriving and events unfolding according to divine plan.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:1 marks Festus’s arrival after three days, showing God’s providential control over political transitions that affect Paul’s mission.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Acts 25:26 specifically demonstrate in the context of legal proceedings?
questions.explanation: In Acts 25:26, Festus acknowledges he has no certain accusation to write to Caesar, demonstrating the attribute of divine justice reflected in human legal honesty.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do verses Acts 25:22 and Acts 25:23 teach about divine providence and the witness of the Church before rulers?
options: God providentially arranges opportunities for the faithful witness before kings and influential leaders.
The Church’s witness is limited to private gatherings and avoids political leaders.
Divine providence removes all opposition to the Church’s message.
The Church’s mission excludes testimony before secular authorities.
questions.correctAnswer: God providentially arranges opportunities for the faithful witness before kings and influential leaders.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:22–23 shows Agrippa’s interest and Paul’s appearance before rulers, illustrating God’s providential orchestration for witness.

questions.question: How does Acts 25:25–27 contribute to the theological understanding of lawful witness and the affirmation of innocence in the face of false accusations?
options: It teaches that a lawful witness must be accompanied by clear accusations; otherwise, innocence is affirmed.
It suggests that accusations alone suffice for condemnation without evidence.
It denies the importance of legal process in spiritual matters.
It encourages silence in the face of false accusations.
questions.correctAnswer: It teaches that a lawful witness must be accompanied by clear accusations; otherwise, innocence is affirmed.
questions.explanation: Acts 25:25–27 shows Festus stating he has nothing certain to accuse Paul of, emphasizing the need for clear charges to justify judgment, affirming innocence otherwise.
